code.title: Four pillars in one small program

followUps: Each pillar shows up in the JDK you use daily. Encapsulation: ArrayList hides its internal Object[] and only lets you change it through add and remove. Abstraction: you code to List and never care how it stores data. Inheritance: ArrayList extends AbstractList and reuses its iterator and equals. Polymorphism: list.size() runs ArrayList.size() or LinkedList.size() depending on the real object.

Inheritance is the most abused, because it looks like the quickest way to reuse code. A subclass becomes tied to the parent's internals, so a change in the parent can break it, and deep hierarchies are hard to read. Example: a Stack extends Vector also exposes insertElementAt, which breaks stack rules. Prefer composition (hold the other object and forward calls) and use inheritance only for a true IS-A relationship with a class built for extension.

code.title: Encapsulation guards state, abstraction hides the provider

followUps: Not necessarily: a class with private fields and a public getter and setter for every field is only encapsulated in name. Anyone can set any value, so the class cannot protect its rules. Example: setBalance(-500) is accepted, so the invariant "balance never below 0" is not guarded. Real encapsulation exposes behaviour (deposit, withdraw) that validates input, and shares only the getters that are actually needed.

Modules (Java 9+) add a level above the class: a package inside a module is hidden unless the module file lists it in exports. Even a public class in an unexported package cannot be used from other modules, and reflection into it is blocked unless the package is opensed. So you can keep com.shop.internal private to the module, and publish only com.shop.api. This is how the JDK hides sun.* internals.

code.title: Overloading chosen at compile time, overriding at runtime

followUps: Because List<Integer> has two methods: remove(int index) and remove(Object o). With an int argument the compiler picks the first one in phase 1 (exact match, no boxing), so remove(1) deletes the element at index 1. In [10, 1, 5] it removes the 1 at index 1 and leaves [10, 5], but in [10, 20, 5] it would remove 20, since it is an index. To remove the value, write list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).

Yes, and it is common. Suppose Parent has greet(Object) and greet(String), and Child overrides greet(Object) and adds greet(Integer). The new one is an overload (different parameters), the other is an override (same signature). The compiler picks among all three by the declared argument type; then the JVM dispatches the chosen signature on the real class. Use @Override so a typo cannot silently create an overload.

code.title: Static hiding, private methods and real overrides

followUps: It calls the static method of the declared type, and does not throw. A static method does not need an object, so the compiler turns ((Parent) null).staticMethod() into Parent.staticMethod(), and the null is never used. Example: Parent p = null; p.who(); prints "Parent.static". This is confusing, so call static methods by the class name, and most IDEs warn about the instance-style call.

Frameworks like proxies generate a new subclass at runtime and can use reflection or bytecode tools that skip the Java language rules. They can call or wrap a private method only through those back doors, and it is not true overriding. Java itself does not allow it because private means "internal detail of this class": a subclass cannot see it, so an equally named method is a different method. Allowing override would let subclasses break the parent's hidden logic.

code.title: Abstract class with template method plus interface

followUps: No, an interface cannot have a constructor, because a constructor initialises instance state, and interfaces have none (only constants). A class implementing it is the one that builds the object. Also an interface is never instantiated on its own, and a class can implement many interfaces, so there would be no clear order for several constructors. If you need shared set-up, use an abstract class with a constructor, or a static factory method on the interface.

Choose a sealed interface when the set of subtypes is small, fixed and known, and you want the compiler to check every case in a switch. Example: sealed interface Result permits Ok, Err with two records. An abstract class fits when subclasses share state or code, and when others may extend it. A sealed interface can also be implemented by records, which cannot extend a class, so it is the best fit for plain data types.

code.title: Default method diamond resolution rules

followUps: No, a default method cannot define equals, because a class always inherits Object.equals, and the rule "class wins" means the class version would always beat the interface default. A default in an interface could never run, so the compiler rejects it. The same applies to hashCode and toString. If you want shared equality logic, put it in an abstract class or a helper static method.

The main risk is that a new default method can clash with or silently change a class that already exists. Example: a library adds default void sort() to an interface, and your class already has an incompatible sort(), or you implement two interfaces that both add hi(); then your code stops compiling (unresolved diamond). Behaviour can also change: a class inheriting a default may now run code that you never tested. Library authors add defaults carefully and document them.

code.title: Dynamic dispatch through an interface

followUps: Not on modern JVMs: marking a method final rarely makes it faster. The JIT compiler already knows whether a method is overridden by checking which classes are loaded (Class Hierarchy Analysis), and it inlines single-implementation calls anyway. So use final for design reasons (to stop overriding), not for speed. The one small gain is that a final method needs no deoptimization guard if a subclass loads later, which is rarely measurable.

Start with JFR or a profiler to find hot methods, then print JIT decisions with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining. A call site that cannot be inlined shows up as "virtual call" or "too many receiver types" (megamorphic). With JITWatch you can read this log visually. Check the hot loop: if one interface call sees 3 or more concrete classes, consider splitting the list by type, or using a switch over a sealed type. Measure with JMH before changing code.

code.title: equals without hashCode breaks HashMap

followUps: Yes, return 42; is legal, because the contract only demands that equal objects give equal hash codes. The consequence is speed: every key lands in the same bucket, so a HashMap with N keys degrades from O(1) to a linear scan of N entries (Java 8+ turns a long bucket into a tree for O(log N) if keys are Comparable). With 100,000 keys that means very slow lookups. Correct but terrible performance.

getClass() requires exactly the same class, which keeps equals symmetric and transitive, but a subclass instance is never equal to a parent one, and some proxies break. instanceof allows subclasses to be equal, which suits an interface-defined equality (like List), but if a subclass adds a field and extends equals, symmetry breaks: p.equals(cp) is true while cp.equals(p) is false. Safer: make the class final and use instanceof, or use getClass().

code.title: Inheritance counts 6, composition counts 3

followUps: java.util.Stack extends Vector, so a Stack can be indexed and modified in the middle (stack.add(0, x)), which breaks the idea of a stack. Properties extends Hashtable<Object,Object>, so you can put non-String values into something meant to hold strings. In both cases the subclass was not a real IS-A of the parent, and composition would have been safer. That is why Deque is recommended over Stack.

A forwarding class holds a reference to another object that implements the same interface and passes every method call straight to it. A CountingSet can then wrap any Set, and count in its own add and addAll. Because the wrapped set's addAll calls its own add, not ours, nothing is counted twice. You depend only on the public contract, not on how the parent is implemented, so JDK changes cannot break it.

code.title: final reference versus an immutable object

followUps: A variable is effectively final if you never reassign it after its first assignment, even without writing final. Lambdas and anonymous classes capture a copy of the value, not the variable itself, so the value must not change, otherwise the copy and the original would disagree and cause confusing bugs (and thread-safety issues). Example: int n = 5; Runnable r = () -> print(n); is fine; adding n++ later is a compile error. To change a value, use an array of length 1 or an AtomicInteger.

Because the compiler copies the value of a compile-time constant (a static final primitive or String initialised with a literal) straight into the client's bytecode. If you change MAX = 10 to 20 in the library and clients are not recompiled, they still use 10. Example: a library constant TIMEOUT = 30 changed to 60 has no effect on old jars. Avoid it by recompiling clients, or by making the value non-constant, for example static final int MAX = Integer.parseInt("10").

code.title: Overridable call in a constructor sees null

followUps: The field is a compile-time constant, so the compiler inlines the number 5 wherever it is used, and it never reads the field. Because of that, the value is right even before the constructor has run. Compare: final int size = 5; prints 5 inside the early call, but final int size = compute(); or a String label = "x" + n would print 0 or null. Constants are only literals or expressions of literals.

JEP 513 (flexible constructor bodies, Java 25) lets you write statements before super(...) or this(...), as long as they do not touch this. You can now validate or compute arguments there, for example if (size < 0) throw ...; super(size);, instead of using static helper methods. You still must not read the instance or call its methods before super(), and the new prologue can even assign subclass fields, so the virtual call problem can be reduced by initialising fields first.

code.title: Multiple inheritance via interfaces and composition

followUps: C++ solves the diamond with virtual inheritance: class B : virtual public A and class C : virtual public A. Then D : public B, public C holds just one A subobject, instead of two. The most derived class (D) is responsible for calling the constructor of A. Without virtual, D has two copies of A and using d.x is ambiguous. It works but adds complexity and a small runtime cost, which is a reason Java chose to avoid state inheritance.

Example: a Duck needs to be both a Flyer and a Swimmer. I made both interfaces, with default methods for common behaviour, and had Duck implement both. For shared state, such as an Engine, I used composition: Duck holds a MotionControl object and delegates to it. That gave multiple types and behaviours without sharing fields, and each part could be unit-tested alone with a fake.

code.title: Square breaks Rectangle (LSP)

followUps: Strictly, yes: Collections.unmodifiableList returns a List whose add throws UnsupportedOperationException, so code written for List that calls add breaks. The JDK documents that these mutators are optional operations, so the contract of List allows it. It is a known trade-off: a cleaner design would use separate read-only and mutable types, which is what List.copyOf plus clear documentation approximate.

A contract test is one test class written against the supertype, run once for every subtype. Example: an abstract ShapeContract that sets width 5 and height 4 and asserts area 20, and a subclass of the test for Rectangle and one for Square. The Square run fails (area 16), so the LSP violation is caught automatically. The same idea works for Comparator, List and any interface you publish.

code.title: Shallow clone vs copy constructor

followUps: A shallow copy is correct when all fields are immutable or primitives, so sharing them cannot cause trouble. Example: a Point with int x, y or an object holding only a String and Integer: copying the references is safe, because nobody can change what they point to. It is also fine when you deliberately want shared state, such as two views on the same cache. If any mutable field is shared by accident, use a deep copy.

Keep a map from original objects to their copies while copying (an IdentityHashMap). When you reach an object, check the map first: if it is already there, reuse the copy, else create the copy, put it in the map, then copy its fields. This stops infinite loops and keeps shared references shared. Cost: O(N) time and O(N) space for N objects. Alternatives are serialization round trips, which are slower, or a library copier.

Node copy(Node n, Map<Node,Node> seen) {
  if (seen.containsKey(n)) return seen.get(n);
  Node c = new Node(n.val); seen.put(n, c);
  c.next = copy(n.next, seen);
  return c;
}

code.title: Sealed records with exhaustive switch

followUps: Adding a permitted subtype makes every switch over the sealed type that has no default fail to compile, until you add the missing case. That is a feature: the compiler lists exactly where to update, so nothing is forgotten. Example: adding record Div(Expr l, Expr r) to Expr breaks eval and show with "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values". A default branch hides this, so avoid it for sealed types.

Make the type hierarchy sealed with records, then write each "visit" as a function that uses an exhaustive switch. You need no accept(Visitor) method and no visitor interface with one method per type. Example: String show(Expr e) { return switch (e) { case Num n -> ...; case Add a -> ...; }; }. New operations are just new functions. The compiler checks that all cases are covered, so it plays the role of the visitor interface with less code.
